analysis.one_liner: Lets states open Medicaid to any resident who wants to buy in at income-based premiums.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since its June 2025 referral, with no action since and no Republican support among its 15 sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill creates a public health insurance option run through Medicaid. Each state could choose to open its Medicaid program to residents who are not already on Medicaid and not enrolled elsewhere, letting them buy coverage at premiums capped at 8.5 percent of household income, with the same federal tax credits and cost-sharing help that apply to marketplace plans. It also gives holdout states the full federal match for expanding Medicaid, requires Medicaid to cover reproductive health care including abortion, and raises Medicaid pay for primary care to Medicare levels.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and under-insured residents in states that opt in, especially people whose employer coverage is unaffordable or whose only other option is a costly marketplace plan. Primary care doctors, clinics, and health centers also gain from Medicare-level reimbursement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured residents and primary care providers

how_it_helps.text: Residents not eligible for Medicaid and not enrolled in other coverage could buy into their state's Medicaid plan starting January 1, 2026, if the state elects to offer it.

Buy-in premiums and cost-sharing would be capped: total premiums per family cannot exceed 8.5 percent of household income, and standard Affordable Care Act cost-sharing limits and reductions would apply.
Buy-in enrollees would be eligible for the same premium tax credits as people buying marketplace plans, with the state Medicaid agency treated as the plan issuer.
The federal government would pay 90 percent of the administrative cost of running a state buy-in program.
Any state that expands Medicaid, no matter how late, would receive the enhanced federal matching rate originally reserved for states that expanded in 2014.
Medicaid would have to cover comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care, including abortion, as a condition of state plan approval.

Primary care furnished under Medicaid by family doctors, OB-GYNs, nurse practitioners, rural health clinics, and health centers would be paid at least 100 percent of Medicare rates, to broaden provider access.

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state budgets bear new costs from the enhanced match, administrative funding, and higher provider payments. Insurers selling individual-market plans would lose customers to the cheaper public option. Enrollees pay premiums, up to the 8.5 percent income cap.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and state budgets; exchange insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill makes abortion coverage a mandatory condition of every state's Medicaid plan, which sharply raises its cost to states and guarantees political opposition that could sink the entire public option.

Federal costs are substantial: a 90 percent administrative match, higher Medicaid primary care payment rates, and the enhanced match for late-expanding states all draw on federal funds without dedicated revenue offsets.
Coverage is optional by state, so residents in states that do not opt in would get nothing, leaving a patchwork rather than a national option.
Premiums of up to 8.5 percent of income could still be too expensive for many uninsured lower-income households who earn too much for free Medicaid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A genuinely meaningful offer: a cheaper, government-run plan with real subsidy support for people priced out of coverage. The costs are real federal spending, and the mandatory abortion-coverage provision makes an otherwise moderate, state-optional bill far harder to pass, trading broader availability for political weight.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the State Public Option Act on June 12, 2025, joined by 14 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance; no further action appears in the record.
Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat; no Republican has signed on.
With Republicans holding the Senate majority and the Finance Committee chairmanship, the referral has produced no committee activity through the end of the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers selling individual-market plans are better off, since a competing public option never advanced, and so are Republican committee leaders, who avoided a vote on a proposal their conference opposes.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing a state-based Medicaid buy-in public option.

for.name: 14 Democratic senators, including Klobuchar, Booker, Durbin, and Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors on introduction day; none acted further on the record.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in June 2025 and has taken no action since — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Controls committee agendas and floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-run committee has left it dormant.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; the record shows no Republican support, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee has not moved the bill.

industries.note: A Medicaid buy-in capped at 8.5 percent of income, with tax credits attached, undercuts the marketplace plans insurers sell; their interest in stopping the bill runs against the interest of people seeking cheaper coverage.

In states that run Medicaid through private managed-care plans, buy-in enrollees may be enrolled in those plans, giving the companies new premium-paying customers; but in individual-market states they lose members to the public option.

industries.industry: Primary care physicians and community health providers
industries.note: The bill sets a Medicaid payment floor at 100 percent of Medicare rates for primary care, which pays providers more and is intended to widen the provider network available to the public.

industries.industry: Federally qualified health centers and rural clinics
industries.note: These clinics are explicitly included in the Medicare-rate payment floor, boosting their Medicaid reimbursement.

analysis.trajectory: A Democratic-only bill sitting idle in a Republican-run committee is very unlikely to advance this Congress. Its realistic path is reintroduction in a future Congress or partial absorption into a larger Democratic health package if the chamber balance changes; as introduced, it will most likely die without a vote.
